narrative:
The model estimated a 35.0% probability that you would be a bad credit risk. That is not a prediction that you will certainly default; it is a risk estimate that exceeded the bank’s approval cutoff for this loan, so your application was denied.

Among the factors that most influenced the decision, your credit history ranked first and actually worked in your favour, pushing the assessment toward good credit rather than bad. The length of the requested credit ranked second and also worked in your favour: at 11 months it is well below the approved average of about 19 months, which the model associates with lower risk. The third most influential factor was your checking account status, and this pushed toward bad credit. A balance of 0–200 DM represents a relatively thin financial buffer, and only about 18% of approved applicants share this status, while many have no account or a stronger balance. The denial reflects the combined effect of all factors, with this checking-account signal adding meaningful upward risk alongside other details in your profile.

Next, ask the bank for the specific policy cutoff and any actionable feedback. Check your credit history for errors, work on reducing existing credit commitments and your installment burden, and build a stronger checking-account or savings buffer before reapplying. Improving those areas can make your profile stronger for a future application.
